description: Back for a second Space Apps, and this year we’re aiming closer to home: the Moon is only 1.3 light-seconds away. We’re taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, building a tool that shows when a landing site has sunlight and a line to Earth, and what happens if the lander misses its target.
summary:
SunSight tells you whether a landing site on the Moon will have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communications, for the whole stay. Choose a site, a date and a mission type, and it draws the full horizon from that spot with the Sun and Earth against the terrain, then gives a plain call: go, marginal or no-go, with countdowns to sunset and to loss of contact.

What sets it apart is the miss test. Landers rarely touch down exactly on target: in March 2025 the Athena lander came down about 250 m from its target, in a crater, and its mission ended within a day. SunSight repeats the calculation at 317 points around the target and shows how much of the nearby ground still works. A built-in game, “Land it yourself”, lets anyone try to find ground that survives.

It runs entirely in the browser on NASA terrain and ephemeris data, and it publishes its own validation, misses included.
details:
What it does

SunSight opens on one sentence: “Land at [site] on [date] for a [mission].” Each part is a picker. Under it is the full 360° horizon as seen from that spot, with the Sun and Earth drawn where a lander would see them, and a call for the whole stay: go, marginal or no-go. “Play the stay” runs the clock forward so you can watch the Sun and Earth move and see when sunlight or contact is lost.

There are 28 cited sites (Apollo, the commercial landers Odysseus, Athena and Blue Ghost, landers from India, Japan, China and the Soviet Union, and Artemis III candidate regions), or you can enter any latitude and longitude. Other views rank the south-pole sites for a date, show one site across a calendar of dates, compare sites side by side, show the terrain in 3D, and share a link to any result.

The miss test

Landers rarely touch down exactly on target, so SunSight repeats the whole calculation on a 50 m grid out to 500 m around the target: 317 points. On our opening example (Shackleton’s rim, 24 July 2029, a 6.5-day crew stay) the target is a go, but only 12 of the 81 points within 250 m still hold. This is a robustness share, not a landing probability. “Land it yourself” turns it into a game: you get three tries to pick a spot, each scored by the same engine, and then the whole ground is revealed.

How it works

  1. Where the Sun and Earth are. NASA/JPL SPICE kernels give the apparent positions of the Sun, the Earth and the three Deep Space Network complexes as seen from the Moon, hour by hour for 2027 to 2030.
  2. What the terrain hides. From NASA’s LOLA elevation maps of the south pole we compute the height of the horizon in 1,440 directions around each point, out to 300 km, for an observer 2 m and 10 m above the ground.
  3. What the lander gets. In the browser, each moment of the stay is tested: how much of the Sun’s disc is above the terrain and not behind the Earth (eclipses included), and whether at least one ground station has a clear line. “Lit” means at least half of the Sun’s disc is visible. Events are timed to the minute.

Three mission presets (robotic lander, 14 days; crew sortie, 6.5 days; long stay, 30 days) set the limits on darkness and on gaps in contact, and every limit can be changed. Only the need for continuous sunlight on a 6.5-day crew stay comes from NASA; the other limits are our own starting assumptions and are labelled as such.

How we know it is right

The Proof page publishes nine checks with their data, and nothing was tuned to pass. Sun and Earth positions agree with JPL Horizons to 0.00003°. Of NASA’s permanently shadowed points in our grids, 433 of 437 (99.1%) never see the Sun in our model. Earth visibility averages 0.23 points above NASA Goddard’s maps (marked partial, because not every outlier is explained). Two checks miss their pass marks and are shown as misses: average sunlight is 2.32 points below NASA Goddard’s maps against a mark of 2, and one of 84 eclipse cases shows 0.09% of the Sun at the edge of totality. More than 400 automated tests cover the code.

Why it matters

Mission planners can screen sites and dates in seconds and see how forgiving a site is before detailed studies. Teachers and the public can see why the lunar south pole is hard: the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so one ridge decides whether a lander has power. The 2025 Athena landing is included as a guided story.

What makes it creative

The horizon is the interface: instead of reading charts, you stand at the landing site and look. The miss test turns a single yes or no into a map of how much error a site forgives. And the game lets anyone feel how small the safe ground is.

Tools

Python (SpiceyPy, NumPy, Numba, Rasterio) for the data pipeline; TypeScript, Preact, Vite and Three.js for the site; pytest, Vitest and Playwright (with axe accessibility checks) for testing; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for hosting. The site is static files: no server, no account, and nothing leaves your device. The code is open source under the MIT licence.

What we considered, and limits

It works on a phone, by keyboard, and with reduced motion. Terrain maps cannot see boulders or craters smaller than a few pixels. Earth contact is geometry only (line of sight), not signal strength, and the Deep Space Network is a reference choice. Sites outside our south-pole terrain grids use a smooth horizon and say so.
